title: When Explicit Instruction Turns Robotic
author: Brendan
summary: Brendan argues that the real difficulty of explicit instruction is not knowing its structure (model, guide, release) but knowing what to do when a lesson does not go to plan, as it rarely does. Schools often respond to that complexity by providing detailed resources, slide decks, scripted programs, textbooks, which is sensible, but when teachers lack a clear mental model of how learning progresses, fidelity collapses into compliance and instruction turns mechanical. He reframes explicit instruction as a decision-making framework organised around Show, Support, and Step Back, and walks through the in-the-moment reads: model again when students hesitate, keep supporting when they can only perform with prompts, return to modelling when errors become consistent, and fade prompts deliberately as accuracy improves. He stresses that responsiveness depends on secure content knowledge, a particular challenge for non-specialist primary teachers, and that schools must make decision rules explicit rather than simply adding resources.
points: The hard part of explicit instruction is not its structure but what to do when students hesitate, err, or fluctuate, which requires real-time decisions.
Resources are not the problem; fidelity without understanding the program's key mechanisms turns instruction into rigid compliance.
Explicit instruction is best understood as a decision-making framework (Show, Support, Step Back) where the real work sits between the phases.
The correct in-the-moment moves depend on the evidence: model again when students hesitate, keep supporting when they need prompts, return to modelling when errors are consistent.
Responsiveness requires content knowledge, so asking non-specialist teachers to be more flexible without supporting subject knowledge is an impossible ask.
quotes: The problem is not knowing what explicit instruction is supposed to look like. The problem is knowing what to do when it doesn’t go to plan.
Without a clear mental model of how learning progresses, fidelity becomes compliance.
The phases matter, but the real work sits between them. If this happens, then do this.
The resource does not decide when to move on. The evidence does.
If explicit instruction ever feels robotic, it is usually because decision making has been replaced with compliance.
To respond well in the moment, teachers need to recognise what an error signals, which example to show next and how to adjust instruction without introducing confusion.
